analysis.one_liner: Gives patients control over who can see, use, and sell their medical records.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 69 House members, was referred to two committees in May 1999 and never received a markup or a vote before Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal standard for how insurers, hospitals, doctors, and other holders of medical records may use and share a patient's identifiable health information. It would give patients the right to see and correct their records, learn who has seen them, refuse blanket consent as a condition of care, and sue violators for damages. It would bar using medical records for hiring, marketing, or insurance underwriting, and would impose civil and criminal penalties for misuse, up to ten years in prison when the motive was profit.
analysis.who_benefits: Every patient whose medical information moves through doctors' offices, hospitals, and insurance companies. Patients would gain the right to inspect and correct their own records, a history of who saw their information, notice of how it is used, and protection from having treatment conditioned on signing away their privacy. The bill specifically excludes employment decisions, marketing, and insurance underwriting as permissible reasons to hand over records, and it shields records from self-pay care from going to insurers. People who report violations would be protected from being fired.

how_it_helps.text: Patients get the right to inspect and copy their records, correct or amend errors, and review a history of every disclosure of their information.
Providers and insurers cannot require patients to sign a broad privacy waiver as a condition of receiving or paying for care.

Disclosing records for employment decisions, marketing, or insurance underwriting does not count as a legitimate health-care purpose, closing the main channels through which medical data reached employers and marketers.
If someone pays for care out of pocket, the provider cannot send that information to an insurer without authorization.

Violations carry civil penalties up to $10,000 per failure, private lawsuits with damages and attorney's fees, and criminal penalties up to ten years in prison when the violation was committed for monetary gain.
Workers who report violations to a government agency are protected from retaliation in hiring, promotion, or discharge.
The bill does not override any state law that gives stronger protection, so state privacy rights would survive.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, health care providers, employers, and companies that gather or trade medical data would bear the cost of building safeguards, keeping disclosure records, and facing penalties and lawsuits for misuse. Compliance with authorization and notice rules would add administrative work to the health system.

drawbacks.text: The bill would add significant administrative and compliance burdens: custodians must build security safeguards, provide notices, obtain informed authorizations, and track disclosure histories, with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per failure attached to each slip-up.

The private right of action, with compensatory damages, $5,000 liquidated damages per action, attorney's fees, and punitive damages for knowing violations, could invite litigation against health care organizations.

Most key rules apply only 'to the extent the Secretary determines appropriate,' leaving the actual stringency of research, oversight, and other disclosures to later regulation rather than the statute itself.

Tighter limits on information flow could add friction to care coordination and insurance payment, though the bill expressly permits disclosures for providing and paying for care, public health, and oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections are broad and concrete: real access rights, limits on the employment and marketing channels where medical data was being exploited, and meaningful penalties. The costs are real but familiar to any regulated information system — compliance work and some litigation risk — and the bill preserves treatment, payment, public health, and research uses. Its main design weakness is the large amount left to the Secretary's discretion. On balance, the benefits to patients' control over intimate information outweigh the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, each committee passed it down to a subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Gary Condit introduced the bill on May 25, 1999, with 28 original cosponsors including Reps. Dingell, Waxman, and Markey, and it was referred the same day to the Commerce Committee and the Government Reform Committee.

On June 4, 1999, it was referred to the Government Reform Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology, and on June 23, 1999, to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
The only further action in the entire Congress was the sponsor's introductory remarks recorded in the Congressional Record on October 31, 2000.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers, employers, and companies that buy and trade medical data were better off: the bill's restrictions on using health records for underwriting, hiring, and marketing never took effect, and the patchwork of state laws described in the bill's own findings remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers holding medical data

for.name: Rep. Gary Condit
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Health Information Privacy Act and kept it alive with floor remarks in October 2000.

for.name: 69 House cosponsors — 68 Democrats, 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including senior committee members such as Reps. Dingell, Waxman, and Markey; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: Rep. Thomas Bliley
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that received the bill and referred it to the Health and Environment Subcommittee, which never reported it out or held a markup.

against.name: Rep. Dan Burton
against.what_they_did: Chaired the second committee of referral; its Government Management Subcommittee received the bill and never acted on it.

against.name: House Commerce and Government Reform Committees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from June 1999 onward without any hearing, markup, or vote recorded in the action history.

sides.party_line_note: All 69 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's sole Independent; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-led committees controlling the bill's path never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would bar using medical records for insurance underwriting and would prohibit sending a self-pay patient's information to a payer without consent, cutting insurers off from data they used to price and deny coverage. Violations would carry civil and criminal penalties.
Disclosing medical records for employment decisions would no longer be a legitimate purpose, ending employer access to worker health information for hiring and personnel decisions.

Providers would face compliance costs, disclosure tracking, and lawsuit exposure, but the bill keeps the treatment and payment disclosures they depend on and replaces the patchwork of inconsistent state privacy laws with a single federal standard.

industries.industry: Health data brokers and direct marketers
industries.note: Marketing would be explicitly excluded from permissible disclosure, obtaining records under false pretenses would be banned, and profit-motivated misuse would carry up to ten years in prison.

The bill would give researchers a clear legal pathway to use records for studies approved by certified review entities, with identifiers destroyed as soon as possible — a defined basis for research that benefits public health.
